title: Parameters of Random Variables
videoTitle: AP Statistics Topic 2.9 Parameters of Random Variables
intro: After this lesson you can find the mean and standard deviation of a discrete random variable, interpret both in context, and find the mean and standard deviation of a transformed random variable.

moments.title: A parameter describes a distribution
moments.text: A single fixed number that summarizes a population or the probability distribution of a random variable.

moments.title: Mean and expected value are the same
moments.text: The average value of the random variable after a large number of repetitions.

moments.title: $\mu_X$ and $E(X)$
moments.text: Two symbols for the same thing. The parentheses in $E(X)$ do not mean multiplication.

moments.title: Horse wins and teeth brushing
moments.text: Long-run averages: 1.415 wins in two races, 135.4 seconds of brushing.

moments.title: The journal picture
moments.text: Imagine writing every result in a journal. The mean is the average of all the entries.

moments.title: Mean of a discrete variable
moments.text: Multiply each value by its probability and add: $\mu_X=\sum x_iP(x_i)$.

moments.title: Continuous: no formula
moments.text: The mean of a continuous variable is given, and comes from the law of large numbers.

moments.title: Standard deviation measures variability
moments.text: The outcome tomorrow may be a bit more or less than the mean. The SD says by how much, typically.

moments.title: SD of a discrete variable
moments.text: $\sigma_X=\sqrt{\sum (x_i-\mu_X)^2P(x_i)}$. It is on the formula sheet and is rarely done by hand.

moments.title: Desmos discrete distribution
moments.text: In the video: Plus, Inference, Probability Distribution, Discrete, then Summary. The embedded calculator on this site has no Discrete option, so the Desmos section uses lists.

moments.title: Interpret mean and SD
moments.text: The mean is the long-run average. The SD is the typical distance from that mean. Use context.

moments.title: Continuous: hippo and lion weights
moments.text: Weight is measured, so the mean and SD are given, not calculated.

moments.title: Change of units
moments.text: Multiply the mean and SD by the conversion factor. 450 lb and 40 lb become 204.5 kg and 18.2 kg.

moments.title: Shirts to dollars
moments.text: At 28 dollars a shirt, the mean and SD are both multiplied by 28.

moments.title: Profit with an 8 dollar fee
moments.text: The mean is multiplied by 28 and has 8 subtracted. The SD is only multiplied.

moments.title: Adding a constant does not change SD
moments.text: Multiplying changes mean and SD. Adding or subtracting a constant changes only the mean.

sections.title: Mean and standard deviation of a discrete variable
sections.intro: Grace sells T-shirts at a craft show. Let $S$ be the number sold in a day, with probabilities 0.08, 0.15, 0.26, 0.35, 0.10, and 0.06 for 0 through 5. The mean is easy by hand. The SD is much faster with technology.
steps: Write the distribution as a table of values and probabilities.
Mean: multiply each value by its probability and add the products.
SD: use technology, because the formula takes one row of work for every value.
Write the symbols and interpret both numbers in context.

parts.label: Standard deviation
parts.text: The video reads this from the calculator summary.

parts.label: Continuous case
parts.text: For a measured variable such as hippo weight, the mean and SD are given.

sections.title: Transform a random variable
sections.intro: Grace earns 28 dollars per shirt and pays an 8 dollar fee to sell at the show. Her profit is $28S-8$. Multiplying changes both the mean and the standard deviation. Subtracting the fee changes only the mean.

parts.label: Standard deviation
parts.text: Only the multiplier counts. The 8 dollar fee does not change the spread.

parts.label: Units
parts.text: Lion mean and SD in kilograms. Divide both by the conversion factor.

sections.title: Desmos walkthrough
sections.intro: The calculator starts empty. Its distribution list has no Discrete option, so you will type the values and probabilities as lists. Work through each task yourself, the way you would on the exam, then check what you observe.

steps.title: Mean and SD from a table
steps.suppose: we want the mean and standard deviation of $S$, the number of shirts Grace sells.
steps.observe: Each row shows its value as you type. The mean is 2.42, and the SD sits just below 1.26.
do: Click an empty row in the expression list and type `S=[0,1,2,3,4,5]`.
On a new row type `total(S*P)` for the mean.
On a new row type `sqrt(total((S-2.42)^2*P))` for the standard deviation.

steps.title: Mean and SD from a graph
steps.suppose: a graph gives $P(0)=0.10$, $P(1)=0.25$, $P(2)=0.30$, and $P(3)=0.35$ for the points $P$ in one play.
steps.observe: Check first that the four probabilities add to 1. Then read the mean and SD from the two rows.
do: Read each bar height as its probability and check they add to 1.
On a new row type `X=[0,1,2,3]`, then on the next row `Y=[0.10,0.25,0.30,0.35]`.
On a new row type `total(X*Y)` for the mean.
On a new row type `sqrt(total((X-1.9)^2*Y))` for the standard deviation.

steps.title: Transform the mean and SD
steps.suppose: each shirt sells for 28 dollars and we want the mean and SD of the revenue.
steps.observe: Compare with the mean and SD if you multiplied each value by 28 in the table. The two answers agree, and the multiplication is much faster.
steps.expected: Mean about $67.76$ dollars, SD about $35.24$ dollars (35.22 if you use the rounded 1.258).
do: On a new row type `2.42*28` for the mean.
On a new row type `1.258*28` for the standard deviation. Use more decimals of the SD from the first step if you like.

steps.title: Profit after the fee
steps.suppose: the profit is 28 times the shirts sold, minus an 8 dollar fee.
steps.observe: The fee lowers the mean by 8 and leaves the SD exactly where it was.
steps.expected: Mean about $59.76$ dollars, SD about $35.24$ dollars.
do: On a new row type `2.42*28-8` for the mean.
On a new row type `1.258*28` for the standard deviation, as before.

sections.title: Write it so it earns credit

traps.title: Interpret the mean in context
traps.better: In the long run, after many days at craft shows, Grace sells an average of about 2.42 T-shirts per day.

traps.title: Interpret the standard deviation in context
traps.better: The number of T-shirts Grace sells in a day typically varies from the mean of 2.42 by about 1.258 T-shirts.

traps.title: Treating the mean as a prediction for one day
traps.weak: Grace will sell exactly 2.42 shirts tomorrow.
traps.better: The mean is the long-run average over many days. Any one day is a whole number and varies around it.

traps.title: Subtracting a constant from the standard deviation
traps.better: Subtracting the fee changes the mean but not the spread. The SD of profit is still about 35.24 dollars.

traps.title: Using the discrete formulas for a continuous variable
traps.weak: Mean of hippo weights = sum of each weight times its probability.
traps.better: A continuous variable cannot be listed, so its mean and SD are given, not calculated from a table.

questions.stem: A discrete random variable $X$ takes the values 1, 2, 3, and 4 with probabilities 0.1, 0.4, 0.3, and 0.2. What is $\mu_X$?
why: 2.5 is the average of the four values and ignores the probabilities.
That is the sum of the probabilities.
That is the average of the probabilities.

questions.stem: The expected number of goals a team scores in a game is 2.4. Which interpretation is best?
opts: The team will score 2.4 goals in its next game
The team scores exactly 2 or 3 goals in every game
After many games, the team's goals per game average about 2.4
In half of its games, the team scores more than 2.4 goals
why: Goals are whole numbers, and the mean says nothing certain about one game.
The mean does not say every game is 2 or 3.
The expected value is the long-run average over many repetitions.
That describes a median, not the mean.

questions.stem: A random variable $X$ has $\mu_X=8.5$ and $\sigma_X=1.2$. Let $Y=3X-10$. What are $\mu_Y$ and $\sigma_Y$?
why: The constant $-10$ shifts the mean but does not change the SD.
The mean needs the $-10$ as well.

questions.stem: Which random variable has a mean and standard deviation that would be given rather than calculated from a table?
opts: The number of heads in three coin flips
The number of customers in a store in an hour
The weight in pounds of an adult male lion
The number of free throws made out of five
why: Counts can be listed in a table.
A count can be listed in a table.
Weight is measured, so it is continuous and its mean and SD are given.
A count out of five can be listed in a table.

sections.title: Write a full response
sections.prompt: During the lunch rush at a food truck, the number of orders $X$ placed in one minute has this probability distribution: $P(0)=0.10$, $P(1)=0.20$, $P(2)=0.35$, $P(3)=0.25$, and $P(4)=0.10$. The truck earns 12 dollars on each order and pays 3 dollars per minute in fees. Let $Y=12X-3$ be the truck's profit in dollars for one minute.
parts: (a) Calculate the mean and standard deviation of $X$.
(c) Find the mean and standard deviation of $Y$ and explain why the standard deviation of $Y$ is not $12\sigma_X-3$.
sample: (b) After many one-minute periods, the number of orders averages about 2.05 orders per minute.

(c) $\mu_Y=12(2.05)-3=21.60$ dollars. $\sigma_Y=12(1.117)\approx13.40$ dollars. Subtracting 3 shifts every value by the same amount, so the spread does not change. Only multiplying by 12 changes the spread.
checklist: (a) Mean calculated with each value times its probability
(b) Long-run average language, with the variable and units
(c) Mean transformed with both the multiplier and the constant
(c) SD multiplied by 12 only, with the reason that adding a constant does not change spread

footer: Built from the video's auto-generated captions. Practice questions are newly written. Means and standard deviations were computed when the page was written.

flags.text: The video gives 0.683 as the standard deviation of the horse's wins, with a mean of 1.415. From the distribution of 0.18, 0.225, and 0.595, the SD is 0.776. The page does not use the video's 0.683.
At about 24:25 the instructor says each shirt cost 20 dollars and that the mean is 2.24 shirts. The scenario uses 28 dollars and the mean is 2.42, as in the transcript's later steps.
The video says the SD 'could vary by' a number. The page uses the exam-style phrase 'typically varies from the mean by about'.

Desmos menu names and labels were checked against the embedded Desmos calculator in November 2026. Steps use the labels on screen: inference, Probability Distribution, Create Distribution, Cumulative Probability with REGION (Inner, Outer, Left, Right) and COMPUTE (Area, Bounds).

The video uses a Discrete distribution with a Summary tab (likely Bluebook's Desmos). The embedded calculator lacks it, so lists and total() are used. Values verified in the embedded calculator: mean 2.42, SD 1.2584.
